notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1445.tmp1445.opp-lat: §2: 'nox lassus et lapsus' read as 'mox lassus et lapsus' (soon, worn out and fallen). §3: 'campo Diram' unidentified (perhaps a corruption; Genesis places the tower in Shinar); the woman who bore 'the sun and fire' is presumably Mary; the virgin who suckled a lion is not identified. §4: 'in jecore amorem, et flatum, et I,vitatem in cursu' appears corrupt; probably something like 'in pulmone flatum et levitatem' has dropped out, so breath and lightness are not properly assigned to the liver. 'senium' and 'senectus' rendered 'elder age' and 'old age'. §5: 'sies'' read 'si est'; 'seu su' read 'sensu'; 'per spem lensa' uncertain, rendered as 'tensa' (intent); 'Iulia' read 'laeta' (glad); 'theoricam ex Heli' taken as the contemplative life from Elijah (Helias), though Heli could be Eli.

Ch. 6: 'principes per Deum' is odd; taken as the prince of angels [made] by God. 'profectus est' read as went down. 'Ite quo labore' (scan damage) read roughly as 'as by toil'. 'plEna' read as poena. Ch. 7: 'vapulandi' marked (sic) in the edition; sense uncertain. Ch. 9: 'molat' read as 'mutat/malat' (worsens); 'strepitat' read for 'strepiiat'; 'debilitat' for 'dehiritat'; 'vastat' or similar for 'ascaiat' (ruins), uncertain; 'negligit mentem' rendered literally. Ch. 10: 'dilat' read as 'ditat' (enriches); 'loquimur' read as 'loquitur'.

§12 'Cadi' read as 'facit'; 'tutio' (sic in edition) taken as 'tuitio', protection; 'auxit nm' read as 'auxilium'. §14: 'pœnitentia' at the start of the sentence on old age is an editorial supplement; the verb 'optat' is carried over. §17: 'Uult' read as 'Ruth'. The names Chacham/Chamna and Adach/Moach are apocryphal, not identified further. 'quae usque ad decimam generationem' follows Deut. 23:3.

Line 18: 'anno uterini' read as 'ambo uterini' (both from one womb); 'Ruth ac Moab' read as 'Ruth de Moab'. The numeral 'iD.' within this line is section 19, and '21).' opening the next line is evidently 20. Line 19: the Hebrew and Greek names are given as the text has them; 'Ruba' presumably stands for Hebrew ruah, 'ageos' for Greek hagios, and 'Bar' (actually Aramaic, 'son') is wrongly called Greek by the author, as is 'Pater' said to mean 'begetter' in Latin. The text breaks off after the gap in the list of the three things created ('angelos, et... et informem materiam').

nodes.text: APPENDIX XXI.
THE BOOK OF NUMBERS,
On which see the Isidoriana, chapter 63, no. 10 and following.

1. With our most high Lord helping, and our most merciful Saviour Jesus Christ granting [it], I wish to write a few things, briefly but usefully, about number and its mystical mystery. What 1, what 2 and 3 say, what 4, what 5 and 6 declare, what 7, what 8, what 9 and 10 relate, and up to 24, if we can get that far, we wish to say what they show.

2. One, then, belongs to God alone, because in all things, and before all things, and above all things, in his omnipotence, and magnificence, and incomprehensibility he is one, just as the divine voice spiritually affirms at the head and beginning of sacred Scripture, saying: Hear, Israel, the Lord God is one. For who in heaven or on earth, or beneath the earth, can be like God alone in eternity, in power, in trinity, in unity, in divinity, in humanity? Therefore one and the same God is called sole, because neither before, nor after, nor then, [nor] now is any other found or read of in heaven or on earth to be like him, since he who in his pride wished to be like him in heaven soon, worn out and fallen, perished, and deserved to be a demon, and Satan, and the prince of demons in hell. Many things, then, among God's creatures and in the sacred Scriptures, which seem to be manifold, are nevertheless called one by one name: such as man, soul, faith, baptism, charity, hope, peace, bread, the Catholic Church, and many others, which I now pass over for the sake of brevity. But about the things we have mentioned, that is, man, and soul, and the rest that follow, even if not in order, we shall nevertheless speak in their proper places, as God grants.

3. From what was man made? We find that one man was made by God in the beginning. We read that from his rib one woman was made; [Scripture] testifies that there was one language to be spoken, that is, Hebrew, until the building of the tower of Nimrod. This tower was built in the plain of Diram. [Scripture] testifies that there was one Abraham, who is also said to have been the head of faith, because from Adam to the birth of Christ no man is found called Abraham; of this Abraham it is said: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. Did not Abel believe, and deserve to be the first crowned with martyrdom? Did not Enoch believe, who still lives in the body? Did not Noah, justified, believe, whom the Lord delivered with the ark and all that were in it? And neither Abel, nor Enoch, nor Noah were called the head of faith. Why is this? That is, although the faith of these righteous men appeared in their time, it was nevertheless rare and always fell short. But from Abraham up to now, and up to the end, faith has not failed, does not fail, and will not fail. Therefore Abraham was called the head of faith. There was one Noah, who built the ark, and whether there was another besides, Scripture is silent. This same Noah was the first after the flood to build an altar to the Lord on the mountains of Armenia, because there among the mountains the water of the flood left the ark. The writings relate that one woman, that is, Lot's wife, was turned into a statue of salt. This statue stands to this day, so that everyone who sees it may fear God and believe him almighty. One woman appeared in the world, such that no other like her was ever born, who carried the sun and fire in her womb for nine months, and it did not harm her to any extent in any way. I have read that one virgin suckled a lion; I do not hesitate to believe it, and I do not cease to marvel. [There is] one greatest mediator between men and God, who on the side of men became true man. Therefore he can truly be called mediator, and could [be], because neither did the divinity harm the humanity, nor was the humanity contrary to the divinity. [There is] one city in heaven, which is the mother of all the saints, which is called Jerusalem and is interpreted 'vision of peace'. Into this city no one who is unworthy, and proud, and impure has entered, enters, or will enter. Thus far we have spoken about one; now we are going to speak about two.

4. Of how many substances does man consist? Man consists of two substances, made in the image and likeness of God, that is, of soul and body only; but in these two substances, joined together into one, many kinds appear to exist. For in the human body nine measures are without doubt combined: that is, four principal ones, which are earth, water, air, fire, and five further kinds following, that is, salt, grass, flowers, stones, clouds; and so that you may understand all these better, read thus: earth in man is the thickness and heaviness of the flesh, water is sweat and saliva. Air is the breathing itself, moist, cold and warm, breathing through mouth and nostrils. Fire in man is what cooks food in the stomach, and [is] in the heat of the blood; salt in the saltiness of blood, and sweat, and tears, and urine, because all these in man are salty. Grass [is] in the hair of the head and body, flowers in the variety of the eyes, stones in weight and hardness, because stones are called the bones of the earth. Clouds [are] the instability of the mind and thoughts. And the body composed of these nine measures, and framed together with greater and lesser bones, is constituted with principal joints numbering 365. For the other, lesser ones a number is scarcely found. Likewise with principal veins, 365, but the lesser veins are innumerable. Also with sinews and blood, flesh and skin, marrow, cartilage, head, and three brains: the first is called memory, the second sense, the third is called motion. With 5 senses, that is, sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch. With 6 ages, that is, infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, elder age, old age: infancy, which ends at 7 years; childhood, which ends at 14 years; adolescence, which extends to 28 years; youth, which ends at 50 years; elder age, which closes with the seventieth year; but old age, which is not completed by periods and number of years, but by toil, and pain, and death. In man, then, there are 10 skilfully made windows. Through the first window he utters words, takes in air and breathes, takes food and tastes. Through two windows he sees far and near; through two others he smells and breathes. Through two other, lower ones he discharges outside what the body must. The tenth window, named the navel, adorns the belly. Man has in the heart understanding and thought, counsel and fear; in the spleen laughter; in the gall anger; in the liver love; and breath, and lightness in running and swimming. By nature the body of man consists of all these, and many others which I pass over for the sake of brevity. The nature of this same body carries four diversities in itself: that is, it hungers, thirsts, desires, sleeps. The use of this nature, then, is fulfilled in four things: that is, eating, drinking, begetting, sleeping. This account of the body has been given briefly; now let the origin of the soul be told.

5. What is the soul? And if it is some thing, from what are souls made? What is it itself, what is its name, what use has it among created things? Does it live, or not? If it lives, what does it contribute to the affections of the universe? Does it lead a blessed life, or a miserable one? What then is the soul? It is not heaven, nor earth, nor air, nor fire, not water, not God, not the stars; it does not come from the soul of the father or of the mother, as many suppose. [It is] not sight, not hearing, not smell, not taste, or any of the other things, which it would be long to mention, that are in heaven or on earth: the soul is none of these. Thus the soul is given from God, made from nothing, and created by God, as the Lord himself says through Isaiah: I made every breath, that is, every soul; and in the Psalm he likewise says: Who fashioned their hearts one by one, that is, souls, because the hearts of men are the lampstands of souls. What the soul is, then, must be said briefly, since God has kept silent [on it] in his Scriptures. The soul is a rational and sentient life, giving life spiritually, and invisibly, and wonderfully to all the inner organs and members of the whole body, inside and out, at the command of its Creator, and in a wonderful way serving the five senses of the body, because it sees through the eyes, hears through the ears, smells through the nostrils, distinguishes flavours through taste, and governs all the members through touch; it subsists spiritually in a fourfold manner, that is, by sense, wisdom, thought, will. Sense pertains to life, wisdom to understanding, thought to counsel, will to defence. For the soul, while it is one thing, thus has many kinds and adornments in itself. When it breathes it is spirit, when it perceives it is sense, when it is wise it is mind (animus), when it understands it is intellect (mens), when it discerns rightly it is reason, when it consents it is will, when it remembers it is memory, when it quickens the members it is soul, when it lives well it has the image of God, when well adorned it is pleasing to God and the angels, when full of good virtues it is the seat of the Trinity. These are the adornments of the soul. Through hearing it believes, through desire it seeks, through wisdom it finds, through prayer it asks, through grace it receives, through humility it keeps, through mercy it comes to meet, through kindness it pardons, through teaching it acquires, through penance it sets in order; through example [it is] beautiful, through knowledge bright, through good zeal free, through meekness smooth, through prudence cautious and clear, through simplicity sincere, through steadfastness sober, through justice upright, through patience long-suffering, through obedience ready, through action clean, through hope intent, through abstinence temperate, through chastity holy, through spiritual joy glad, through confession open, through martyrdom adorned, through unity catholic, through concord peaceable, through love of neighbour generous, through the love of God perfect. These are the adornments of the soul. The necessities of the body are these: in hunger food, in thirst drink, in toil rest, in weariness sleep, in delight and in tedium song, in pain health, in weakness strength, in fear refuge, in darkness light, in war peace, and many others which it would be long to tell now for brevity's sake. So, just as human flesh cannot live happily without these necessities, so the soul cannot stand perfectly in the body without what it needs. For the food of the soul is the divine commandment, its drink pure prayer, its bath lawful fasting, its clothing almsgiving from one's own substance, its instrument continual praise of God, its rest perfect poverty, its health infirmity of the body, its refuge pure penance, its peace full charity. O man, whoever you are, constituted, as we said before, of these two substances, that is, body and soul, imitate Christ and the holy Fathers who went before you: learn humility from Christ, devotion from Peter, charity from John, obedience from Abraham, hospitality from Lot, long-suffering from Isaac, endurance from Jacob, patience from Job, chastity from Joseph, meekness from Moses, constancy from Joshua, kindness from Samuel, mercy from David, abstinence from Daniel, almsgiving from Tobias, the contemplative [life] from Elijah, the active from Paul, tearful penance from Mary Magdalene, pure confession from the thief, martyrdom from Stephen, generosity from Lawrence.

6. On pride and envy. That there are two roots, pestilent and deadly to all living things, is not in doubt. From them have arisen all iniquity, and all impiety, and all calamity, and all cruelty, and all tempest, and all pain, and all plague, and all punishment, and all disease, and all mortality, and all tribulation, and every evil whatever that can be found and felt in heaven, on earth, and in hell; one root is called pride, the other is called envy. For who among the wise and those who understand the Scriptures does not know that pride is the root and queen of all evils, as Scripture testifies and says: The beginning of all sin is pride? For through it, first of all, the prince of the angels [made] by God, who was then called Lucifer and seemed like the seal of the living God, went down from the throne of the Most High, and from the height of heaven, and from that great and holy city which is called vision of peace, in which are the nine orders of angels, together with a tenth part of the angels into the depths of hell. O thing so cruel and so evil, beyond belief! That most hardened dragon, deceiver of himself and inventor of death, in his very casting-down found the second root of the death of all, which is called envy. For thus sacred Scripture says: Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world. In this way, then, sin first entered through envy, and through sin death took its origin; that is, it arose from the wicked suggestion of the most cruel enemy. From the wicked suggestion a depraved thought burst forth within, and the depraved thought gave birth to delight, delight to consent, consent to action, action to habit, habit to necessity, necessity to an evil death, evil death to perdition. So by the suggestion of the devil through the serpent Eve was led astray, and thus the first man, Adam, led astray through Eve, transgressed the commandment of his Creator, and in that very transgression found toil and death, and left them behind him to his offspring, as by toil and death God said to Adam: In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread; and again he says: You are earth, and into earth you shall go. And Scripture, affirming this, says: As death was given in Adam, so it will rule over all his sons. Having thus found toil, and death, and misery, and corruption, and curse, and having left these and countless other things to his progeny, he himself with his offspring was held in darkness and torments from the day of his death in the first age of the world until the resurrection of Christ.

7. That there are two ways, of life and of death, in this world is not in doubt: one by which the saints proceed happily, the other by which sinners destroy themselves. Of these ways the Holy Spirit says thus in the first psalm: The Lord knows the way of the just, and the path of the wicked will perish. The way of the saints is the Lord himself, as he himself said: I am the way, and the truth, and the life; but the way of sinners is the darkness of death, as is read in the Psalm: Let their way, that is, [the way] of sinners, be darkness and slipperiness. The way of the saints is the catholic faith, the way of sinners depraved unbelief; the way of the saints is right hope, the way of sinners barren despair; the way of the saints is perfect charity, the way of sinners hateful iniquity; the way of the saints is the diligence of one who acts, the way of sinners negligence of heart; the way of the saints is the fear of God, the way of sinners transgression of the commandment; the way of the saints is good will, the way of sinners evil desire; the way of the saints is continual prayer, the way of sinners evil wordiness; the way of the saints is confession of frailty, the way of sinners excuse of iniquity; the way of the saints is pure simplicity, the way of sinners dark obscurity; the way of the saints is steadfast patience, the way of sinners temporal instability; the way of the saints is true humility, the way of sinners defiled pride; the way of the saints is temperate abstinence, the way of sinners dissolute excess; the way of the saints is holy chastity, the way of sinners unclean lust; the way of the saints is comely sobriety, the way of sinners besotted drunkenness; the way of the saints is generosity in giving, the way of sinners avarice in hoarding; the way of the saints is the reticence of keeping silent, the way of sinners the loquacity of [one who deserves] beating (sic); the way of the saints is remembrance of good, the way of sinners forgetfulness of God; the way of the saints is holy reading, the way of sinners presumptuous grumbling (sic); the way of the saints is justice and truth, the way of sinners lying and depravity; the way of the saints is the concord of peace, the way of sinners the discord of dissension; the way of the saints is to give thanks in all things, the way of sinners always to despise; the way of the saints is good zeal in the love of God, the way of sinners evil zeal and love of the world; the way of the saints is good showing, the way of sinners evil display; the way of the saints is to lay up treasure in heaven, the way of sinners hiding in the depths; the way of the saints is the humility of Christ, the way of sinners the pride of the devil; the way of the saints is love of the life to come, the way of sinners love of the life that will perish. In the one, what is loved here is taken away; in the other, what is loved is held for ever.

8. We also read in the Scriptures of two hells: one on earth, in which the saints are tested, the other beneath the earth, in which demons and the wicked are damned. Although they are called by one name, they differ greatly from each other; for in the one there is toil and rest, in the other always misery, to which there is no end. In the hell of the saints there is saving compunction, in the hell of sinners penal torment; in the hell of the saints true penance, in the hell of sinners late penance; in the hell of the saints merciful remission, in the hell of sinners just damnation; in the hell of the saints testing with consolation, in the hell of sinners punishment without intermission; in the hell of the saints affliction and refreshment, in the hell of sinners torment always; in the hell of the saints hope of receiving a reward, in the hell of sinners despair of the punishment ending; in the hell of the saints a sweet yoke, in the hell of sinners the heaviness of enduring; in the hell of the saints fear of offending, in the hell of sinners vengeance for transgression; in the hell of the saints toil and rest, in the hell of sinners injury ever penal; in the hell of the saints visiting of the sick, in the hell of sinners forgetfulness of visitation; in the hell of the saints the weeping of penitents, in the hell of sinners tears and gnashing of teeth; in the hell of the saints night and day, in the hell of sinners the outer darkness; in the hell of the saints the good are tested, in the hell of sinners the depraved are punished; in the hell of the saints fire is seen and serves, in the hell of sinners it is possessed and torments; in the hell of the saints angels keep guard, in the hell of sinners the adversaries are tormented; in the hell of the saints grace, kindness and mercy, in the hell of sinners bitterness, wrath and indignation; in the hell of the saints the saints are helped, in the hell of sinners demons and the wicked are damned; in the hell of the saints [there are] good and bad (sic), in the hell of sinners nothing good is held; in the hell of the depraved there is no end of evils, in the hell of the saints there is hope of the kingdom of heaven.

9. On drunkenness. I have found two things, and know them well, in wretched human life, much opposed to each other: one is called drunkenness, the other is called sobriety. Of their opposition I shall say a little briefly. Drunkenness is quite useless: an unworthy thing in men, shameless in women, disgraceful in slaves, reprehensible in priests; it destroys dignity in kings, forgets truth in judges, blots out mercy in the rich, worsens bad habits, throws the whole man into confusion, recalls enmities, stirs up slaughters and disasters, prepares parricides among kinsfolk, raises quarrels, makes the sane mad, makes the wise foolish, renders the sober senseless, washes away memory, cuts off sense, neglects the mind, confounds the understanding, rouses lust, tangles speech, corrupts the blood, impairs sight, deafens the ears, makes laughter noisy, upsets the bowels, shouts indecently, does not speak correctly, moistens the brain, demands sleep, weakens the limbs, hinders the mysteries, dries the throat, wastes the marrow, makes promises in the evening and lies in the morning, ruins body and soul, and destroys all health.

10. On sobriety. Sobriety, however, is useful in all things; it is good in heaven and on earth, good on the way and in the homeland alike; it restrains the young, honours the old, lengthens life (sic), enriches the heir, makes offspring fruitful, increases honour; it is dignity in men, modesty in women, grace in slaves, beauty and praise in priests, glory and victory in kings; it shows truth in a judge, patience in a poor man, generosity in a rich man, brings on good habits, preserves the whole man, renews friendships, calms quarrels, reconciles the discordant, makes the sane serene, adorns the wise, instructs the fool, guards the sober, retains memory, enlightens hearts, makes the mind sincere, sharpens the understanding, cheers the face, composes the countenance, despises lust, overcomes vice, opens the ears, relieves the brain, keeps silent at the right time, speaks correctly, heals the veins, strengthens the blood, waters the bones, nourishes the marrow, strengthens the limbs, enjoys sleep, opens the sight, restrains laughter, shows the mysteries in few words, sparing in speech, faithful in deed; it cleanses body and soul together, and guards all health.

11. On peace and discord. I have truly seen two other things, which differ greatly from each other; if one of them had reigned alone, and the other had not come at the right time, no human being would have lived happily. Of these I wish to say a little, because I am now hastening to other matters. One is called discord, and the other is called peace. Discord is much to be feared, and to be utterly shunned by every Christian; it does these things: out of sons of God it makes sons of the devil, out of friends enemies, out of brothers adversaries; from it [come] whispering, complaint, fury and anger, contention and lying, oath-taking and perjury, injury and scandal, deceit and envy, spite and murder. Discord is nothing other than the separation of peace and the breaking of unity, the teaching of the devil, the way of death, the loss of life, the shattering of the commandments, the alteration of sense, the scattering of understanding, the house of the devil, the path of hell, the expectation of punishment, the expulsion of pardon, the overthrow of discipline, the contempt of charity, the suppression of humility, the disturbance of the mind, the confusion of the limbs, a deadly evil, the venom of the serpent, the bite of the viper, the breath of the basilisk, the vomit of the *regulus* [a kind of serpent], the shutting of the kingdom, the opening of hell, the enemy of God, the friend of the devil.

12. Peace, however, does not act so, for it makes God near to man and man near to God; therefore true peace is to be held, and to be preserved by all Christians in heart and body. For such a mistress is sweet and exceedingly to be loved, who works many miracles; and she is wonderful, who makes out of sons of the devil sons of God, out of enemies friends, out of adversaries brothers, out of strangers kinsfolk, out of outsiders members of the household; from her [come] sincerity and simplicity, mildness and gentleness, meekness and forgiveness, plainness and truth, silence and justice, steadfastness and patience, love and protection (sic), help and healing. Peace is nothing other than the house of God; for so God himself said to his disciples: My peace I give to you, peace I leave to you. What else is peace but nearness to God, the grace of God and union with God, the health of sense, the keenness of understanding, the house of God, the path of the kingdom, the expectation of rewards, the gathering of diligence, the firmness of discipline, the perfection of charity, the circle of humility, the shield of tranquillity, the restraint of rule, the serenity of the limbs? O, if it had been granted me to proclaim peace fully and plainly! I should have had to write many lines with my fingers; for it surpasses all understanding. Its life-giving, honey-flowing sweetness is the opening of the kingdom, the shutting of hell, the friend of God, the enemy of the devil; it is happiness in the present life, joy and gladness in the everlasting life.

13. True penance is recognised in two ways: the first way is to bewail one's misdeeds most devoutly and with most abundant tears, and to repent. The second way is not to commit again what must be bewailed and repented. Penance (poenitentia) is named as if 'punishment' (punitentia), because a man punishes in himself what he did wrongly. The servant of God ought to have such remembrance of sin that he always bewails with tears what he has done. Nothing is worse than to recognise a fault and not bewail it; for every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in penance: because through negligence he did not do good, or because through boldness he committed evil. For what he ought to have done he did not do, and what he ought not to have done, that he did. He does penance worthily who laments his guilt with lawful satisfaction, that is, by condemning and bewailing what he has done, the more deeply the more prone he was to sinning. For great is the power of tears, which without voice or the sound of words obtain the pardon which they ask for faults. For Peter burst into tears; he prayed nothing aloud. I find that he wept; I do not find what he said; I read of his tears, I do not read of his satisfaction. Peter rightly wept, for what is usually defended can be excused; what cannot be defended can be washed away. For tears wash away the offence that it is shameful to confess aloud; so tears, in weeping, look to both modesty and salvation; they do not blush in obtaining, and they obtain what they rightly ask in entreating.

14. Tears, I say, go forth somehow silently; they ask pardon and earn it; they do not plead the case, and they obtain mercy. The prayers of tears are surely more useful than those of words, for speech in praying may perhaps deceive, tears do not deceive at all. For speech sometimes does not set out the whole matter, tears always betray the feeling. O tears, how sweet, how strong, how precious, how pleasant you are at the breasts of mother penance! For as a loving mother gives milk from her breast to an infant, so loving penance offers tears from the compunction of the heart to the penitent. The mother suckles the infant that it may grow; penance gives tears to the penitent that he may come back to life. The mother wishes for the infant that it may live to old age; [penance wishes] for the penitent that he may grow old in no evil. The mother does not wish life to all; penance wishes salvation to all. O penance, great are your breasts, full of the wine of compunction, with which you refresh the guilty, raise the fallen, call back the fleeing, strengthen the broken, cleanse the diseased, wash the lepers, invigorate the weak, gladden the sad, comfort the despairing, heal the wounded, bind up the torn, restore the lost, raise those dead in sins. O penance, what shall I say of you? I cannot praise you as I wish, for you are more precious than refined gold. For through you death is destroyed and the devil is put to flight; through you life is found and God is found; through you hell is shut and the kingdom is found. So he does worthy penance who bewails past things in such a way that he does not commit them again in future; for a repeated wound heals more slowly. The repetition of sin is a grave evil, as if disease came upon disease, as if rain fell upon rain; for he who laments a sin and commits the sin again is as if someone were to wash an unbaked brick: the more it is washed, the more mud it makes. Let no one, then, doubt the goodness of God, let no one despair of the mercy of God; let him seek pardon with his heart, and he will receive it. Let him repent in body and mind, and call God forth to mercy. David after his fault sang a psalm, and did not lose the kingdom, and found pardon. Manasseh, the impious king, wept before the Lord, and won peace for himself and the people. Zacchaeus climbed into a tree, and found salvation. Mary wept, and earned pardon; Peter wept bitterly, and did not lose grace, and obtained pardon. The thief with one word entered paradise with Christ. Longinus opened the side of the Saviour with a lance, and not only found pardon but earned the honour of a bishopric and the glory and crown of martyrdom.

15. On two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets, that is, love of God with all the powers of body and soul, and love of one's neighbour as oneself. One believes in two ways, that is, with perfect faith and perfect working. The cross is carried in two ways, that is, when the body is afflicted by abstinence, or the mind is distressed by compassion for one's neighbour. Divine speech is distinguished in two ways, that is, either the Lord speaks by himself, or words are formed through an angelic creature.

16. There are two kinds of righteous in this life: one, namely, of those who live well but teach nothing; the other of those who live rightly and teach the same right things. Divine striking is understood in two ways, that is, in a good sense: one, by which we are struck in the flesh so that we may be amended in soul and mind; the other, by which we are wounded in conscience out of charity, so that we may love God more ardently. God looks upon men in two ways, that is, either for pardon or for punishment: for pardon, as he looked upon Peter; for punishment, as upon Sodom and Gomorrah.

17. Two thieves were crucified with Christ, that is, Dismas on the right, Gestas on the left. Other names of the thieves [are] Chacham and Chamna. Lot, the son of Abraham's brother, had two daughters, of whom one was called Adach, who bore to her father a son named Moab, from whom the Moabites sprang. The other, who was called Moach, likewise bore to her father a son named Ammon, from whom the Ammonites came. These two sons were not born without guilt, for the father had his daughters as wives, and not will but drunkenness did this; and so the guilt came about in a strange way, that the father had his daughters as wives, and sisters were made mothers to their brothers, and the sons were brothers to their mothers, because the daughters were born of the father's seed, and again of the father's seed sons were begotten in the daughters; and therefore this progeny earned a great curse, and did not enter the Church of God until the tenth generation. And yet Ruth the Moabitess was a good woman, who earned a share in the lineage of Christ. For she was the mother of David's grandfather; for David was the son of Jesse, Jesse the son of Obed, Obed the son of Boaz, and his mother was Ruth. For a grandfather is the father of one's father.

18. Isaac had two sons; one was rejected by God, and the other was chosen. For so Scripture says: Jacob I have loved, and Esau I have hated; and this not without cause, for both were sons of a good father, and both brothers from one womb, in the womb of a good mother, and yet the chosen one supplanted the rejected one in their mother's womb, and seized from him the birthright and the father's blessing. But God willed this to be so for this reason: all the elect sprang from Jacob and from his seed. And yet God did not abandon the rejected one, for Job, both a servant of God and a king, sprang from his line. And I have briefly recalled this because the wicked spring from the good, and the good from the wicked. The wicked from the good: demons from angels; the good from the wicked: saints from the gentiles. The wicked from the good: Ishmael from Abraham, Moab and Ammon from Lot; the good from the wicked: Abraham from the Chaldeans. The wicked from the good: Dathan and Abiram from Levi, Hophni and Phinehas from Eli. The good from the wicked: Ruth from Moab, and Rahab from Canaan. The wicked from the good, which I ought to have said before: Cain from Adam, and Ham from Noah. The good from the wicked: Jonathan from Saul. The wicked from the good: Absalom from David. What more shall I say? For so it will be until the end, the wicked from the good and the good from the wicked; but when he comes who alone is good, he will separate the good from the wicked. 19. We read of two men still living; but where they are, living and hidden, we do not know. One was the seventh from Adam, and named Enoch; the other is Elijah, who was carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot. We have spoken briefly of the two, yet enough, for we are hurrying on to the three.

20. The three persons of the Trinity, in one power and majesty, Father, Son and Holy Spirit; these three persons are called among the Hebrews thus: Abba, Ben, Ruba. Among the Greeks, however, Pater, Bar; but how 'Spirit' is said in Greek I have not yet found. They do, however, say ageos, which in Latin means 'holy'. Abba is father, Ben son, Ruba Holy Spirit. Pater, however, is Greek, and in Latin means 'begetter'. Bar in Greek is 'son' in Latin. So it is called Trinity on account of the distinctness of the persons, but unity on account of the inseparable substance of the deity. He is called Father because he has a Son, and all fatherhood which is in heaven and on earth is named in him and from him. He is called Son because he has a Father, and the Holy Spirit because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. He is called God on account of his power and love; he is called Lord on account of his lordship; he is called almighty because he can do all things, and nothing is impossible for him. And if God is almighty, what is it that he cannot do? That is: he cannot be deceived, he cannot die, he cannot sin. Through the Father we live, move and have our being; through the Son we have reason, knowledge and understanding; through the Holy Spirit we are enlightened with all good gifts. God is spoken of in three ways, that is: essentially, as Paul says: Who is blessed for ever; by appellation, as the Lord says to Moses: I have made you a god to Pharaoh; falsely, as it is said: Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish. In the beginning God created three things, that is, angels, and [...] and formless matter. (The rest is missing.)
